basics.name: Xiangjian Zeng
basics.label: Ph.D. Student, Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
basics.summary: To research brain physiology with computational modeling and create a functional neuromodulation system with engineering toolsets.

work.name: Lewis Lab, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
work.summary: Closed-loop Auditory Modulation of Cerebrospinal Fluid during Sleep
highlights: Develop a closed-loop neuromodulation system that performs real-time scalp-EEG filtering and machine-learning-based slow-oscillation phase prediction to deliver precisely timed auditory stimulation during sleep
Integrate simultaneous EEG-fMRI with electrophysiological and CSF-flow analyses to quantify stimulation-evoked brain and fluid dynamics across younger and older adults
Co-authored a Science Translational Medicine study showing that closed-loop auditory stimulation targeting sleep slow waves modulates cerebrospinal fluid flow in humans

work.name: Insanally Lab, University of Pittsburgh
work.summary: Bayesian ensemble neural decoding and spiking recurrent neural network simulation
highlights: Developed a probabilistic ensemble neural decoder, combining inter-spike-interval-based conditional probabilities across multiple neurons to jointly predict behavioral trial conditions, revealing that traditionally neglected quiet non-classically responsive neurons interact with responsive neurons in learning
Demonstrated that aggregating non-classically responsive population activity improved behavioral decoding accuracy from 60% to 65% during late-stage learning compared with early learning
Built spiking recurrent neural-network models with 1000 units in Python and Julia under biological constraints to simulate cortical mechanisms underlying auditory discrimination behavior
Investigated how flexible neural-network dynamics emerge from balanced excitatory and inhibitory activity and authored a manuscript describing the resulting computational model

work.name: Chamanzar Lab, Carnegie Mellon University
highlights: Developed an automated, non-destructive characterization system for photonic waveguides used in neural optical probes by integrating robotics, computer vision, and signal processing
Demonstrated waveguide-loss characterization previously achievable primarily through destructive methods and first-authored a peer-reviewed conference proceedings paper describing the pipeline

work.name: Lerman Lab, UC San Diego
work.summary: Adaptive neural signal processing and peripheral nerve magnetoneurography
highlights: Led development of an adaptive filtering algorithm for suppressing power-line interference in peripheral nerve recordings and implemented the method in a hardware demonstration
Achieved approximately 45 dB suppression of 60 Hz interference and presented the work as first author at the North American Neuromodulation Society meeting
Developed MATLAB signal-cleaning and processing pipelines for magnetic measurements of peripheral nerve activity, contributing analyses to a collaborative publication
Supported human neuroscience studies involving peripheral nerve measurements and electrical stimulation

work.name: Spitzer Lab, UC San Diego
highlights: Developed an automatic cell recognition program for fluorescence brain slices in Matlab utilizing correlation to count and map a variety of brain cells, obtaining an accuracy close to expert manual selection

work.name: Neuroelectronics Group, La Jolla, San Diego
highlights: Designed, assembled, and tested an Altium PCB for an amplifier used in in vivo neural recording
Reduced the redesigned amplifier-board footprint to approximately 3 cm x 1 cm, more than twofold smaller than the previous design
